samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers reframe 'validate' around a build, pilot or drop decision, and both put past-behavior interviews and existing data ahead of a survey. A is better because it is more proportionate. It keeps the fake door optional and depends on engineering and VP approval. It also states plainly what the tickets can show and what only interviews can, and it lists the steps a human must do. B commits to a fake-door test in week 2 that may not fit the time or resources. B's best point is asking which kind of insurance the VP means, and it also states the limits of the evidence clearly. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B names the decision (build, pilot or drop) and explains why a small study is enough. It separates what support tickets and booking data can show from what only interviews can, says what would shift the recommendation, and lists the steps a person must do. A is solid and practical too, but it is less clear about who does what, and it slots a fake-door test into week 2 without noting that it needs engineering time and the VP's approval.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is the stronger answer. It splits 'validate' into two questions: is there a real problem, and will people pay. It says outright that interviews can't answer the second one, and it has the VP set the threshold instead of inventing one. It also lists the steps a human must do and gives a clear two-week schedule. A is solid and practical, with a good fake-door test and feasibility check, but it uses illustrative prices and a 'few hundred sessions' heuristic. It also never states plainly which steps need a human. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers reframe 'validate', check existing data first, ask about past behavior, and treat a fake-door test as the real purchase signal. A is more careful not to invent numbers: it has the VP set the threshold and reports results as 'n of N'. A also lists what a human has to do and ends with a clear day-by-day table. B adds useful points about sitters and confirmation bias, but it uses invented price figures and claims 'a few hundred sessions' gives a signal, and it says less about who does each step.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A frames the decision more clearly, keeps existing data separate from interviews, and has an explicit section on what a human must do. It also avoids made-up figures and reports findings as 'N of 8'. B is also practical and warns that stated intent is weak evidence, but it adds unsupported benchmarks (an add-on at 8–15% of booking value, click thresholds of 5% and 2%) and never clearly lists the human-only steps. B also squeezes a fake-door test into two weeks, which is a tight fit for the designer's time. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B is better. It names the decision the meeting has to make, splits validation into three questions and says what result would mean stopping or going ahead. It also says plainly what a human must do and avoids made-up numbers, reporting results as 'N of 8' instead of percentages. A is practical and gives a clear two-week plan, but it uses figures with no source (an add-on at 8–15% of booking value, click thresholds of 5% and 2%) and never says outright which steps need a person.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are single paragraphs of roughly 90 words with no lists, preamble or closing offer, and both correctly contrast observing a few people to learn why with measuring many users on a metric to learn which version wins. A adds the useful point that A/B testing needs traffic, while B notes that usability tests work on rough prototypes and ends with a memorable framing. Neither invents statistics, so the two are effectively equal. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs of about 90 words with no lists, preamble or closing offer. Each correctly contrasts a usability test, which watches a few people to learn why things go wrong, with an A/B test, which compares two versions on a metric across many live users to see which wins. A adds that usability tests work on rough prototypes and B adds that A/B tests need traffic, so neither is clearly stronger.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs of about 90–94 words, with no lists, preamble or invented figures, and both describe the two methods accurately. B is slightly better because it says outright that an A/B test shows which version wins 'but not why', which makes the contrast with usability testing clearer. A's 'In short' sentence mostly repeats what it has already said. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (about 90 and 94) and correctly separate a qualitative usability test from a quantitative A/B test, without preamble or invented figures. A is slightly better because it says outright that an A/B test shows which version wins 'but not why'. A also names the methods in its last sentence, where B uses the vaguer 'the first' and 'the second'.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (about 96 for A and 90 for B), with no preamble or invented figures, and both get the qualitative-versus-quantitative distinction right. A matches the rubric more closely by saying participants try to 'complete tasks'. Its closing line also gives the friend a practical rule of thumb for when to use each method, which B lacks. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are single paragraphs under 100 words (about 90 for A and 96 for B), are accurate, and add no padding or invented figures. B says outright that usability participants 'complete tasks', which matches the rubric more closely. It also ends with a clear rule of thumb on when to use each test, which helps someone new to product work.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): A's screener asks more about recent, concrete behavior: what the person did in the past month or last week, and what they actually use to track the queue. It also hides the qualifying answers by keeping the app out of the invitation and adding decoy options. B's intro names the walk-in and no-show product, and its leading yes/no questions (such as 'Does your clinic accept walk-ins?') make it easy to guess the right answers; B's recruiting plan is a little stronger, but that doesn't make up for the weaker screener. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B hides the topic from respondents and uses distractor options. It also screens out industry insiders and frequent research participants, and asks about concrete recent events such as the last week, the last month and the last busy moment. A is solid, and its recruiting plan is somewhat more concrete. However, A's intro reveals the topic (walk-in queues and missed appointments), which tips off respondents, and it lacks exclusions for industry insiders and frequent participants. Both answers say clearly that they can't recruit anyone and neither invents participants, but B's screener design is stronger.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B's screener asks about specific recent events (the last no-show and the last walk-in rush) and hides what qualifies. It uses a generic study description, distractor options and hand-screened open-text answers. A's intro reveals the product, the rural focus and the target role, and several of its yes/no qualifiers are easy to game. Both clearly say they can't recruit anyone and give sensible channels. B also covers consent, incentive placeholders and its sampling limits more thoroughly, while A gives a useful dated timeline. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A's questions ask about recent behaviour, such as the last no-show and the last walk-in rush. Its study description doesn't name the product and doesn't say 'rural', and its distractor options hide which answers qualify. Answer B's intro names the product and the rural target, and several of its yes/no terminate questions make the qualifying answer obvious. B also makes unsupported claims about incentives and panel show rates. Both say clearly that they can't recruit and give practical channels, but A handles consent, the incentive and the deadline more carefully, without inventing figures.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Answer A's questions ask about recent behavior (past two weeks, last month), and it hides the qualifying answers among distractor options. It also warns against naming the topic in the invitation, and it gives a candid warning about the deadline with fallback options. Answer B's intro, outreach blurb and walk-in question reveal the study topic. It also offers a confident timeline without a clear warning that the deadline is tight, and it excludes the user's own clinic contacts while recommending their own network as the first channel. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B asks about specific recent behavior, such as tasks done in the past two weeks and no-shows in the last month. Its first question mixes in distractor options, and it tells the user to keep the topic out of the invitation, so candidates can't guess which answers qualify. It also covers consent, protecting patient privacy during sessions, who the screener leaves out, and realistic fallback plans for the Friday deadline. A is solid and practical, but its intro, outreach blurb and direct questions (for example, a 'Never' walk-ins answer screens people out) reveal what qualifies, and it says less about consent and the deadline risk.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B groups the tickets correctly, with bars showing 4/2/1/1/1 of 9, and it has a clear bottom line, short quotes taken word for word from the tickets and a clean hierarchy. A gets the theme counts right but shows a wrong '5 of 9' stat tile and then a visible note correcting it, which looks unpolished and confuses the numbers. Both screenshots cut off before the recommendations and any caveats, so neither visibly covers rubric item 2 (limits of the evidence), and item 3 can only be partly judged. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A groups the tickets correctly (4, 2, 1, 1, 1), quotes accurately and reads cleanly, with a clear bottom line and count bars. B also has the right theme counts and accurate quotes, but its headline tile says "5 of 9" and then admits underneath that this is wrong, which hurts its credibility and polish. Neither screenshot shows a statement about the limits of the evidence, and the ranked actions are cut off or not visible in both.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get the counts right and quote the tickets accurately. B is better: it lists all five themes separately with counts and bars, gives a clear bottom line based on ticket counts, and keeps what customers said apart from what the team should do. A puts suggested actions inside each finding and lumps lateness and the missing sock into one 'service issues' group. Neither visible part says that the counts only reflect people who wrote to support in one week, and both screenshots are cut off, so B's action list could not be checked. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A's counts match the data exactly (4, 2, 1, 1, 1), it keeps findings apart from conclusions, and its light layout with a clear order of importance works well as a page to send the team. B's counts are also correct, but it merges lateness and the missing item into one 'Service issues: 2' tile and puts its suggested actions inside the findings, so it doesn't separate what the tickets say from the ranked decisions. Neither visible screenshot says that these are only people who wrote to support in one week, so the counts don't show how common each problem is; both quote the tickets accurately and invent nothing.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers group the tickets correctly (4 rescheduling, 2 bag fee, and 1 each for lateness, the missing item and praise), and both quote only text that appears in the tickets. Neither visible portion says that these tickets reflect only one week of people who wrote to support. Both screenshots cut off before the recommendations, so the scores for items 2 and 3 rest only on what is visible. A edges ahead: it uses colour to separate the two main issues from the single-ticket ones, and its 'Suggested next steps' section is visible, which keeps findings apart from actions. B's dark theme is less suited to a summary sent to a team, and its recommendations are not visible. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers group the tickets correctly (4/2/1/1/1) and quote only real ticket text. In the visible part of the screenshots, neither one says the counts only reflect people who wrote in during one week. B keeps 'What we heard' apart from a separate 'Suggested next steps' section and uses colour to show priority, so the findings and the actions are easier to tell apart. B does add a small unsupported claim that the missing sock was 'handled as a normal service claim', and both screenshots are cut off before their recommendations, which limits how firmly items 2 and 3 can be scored.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both kept all the counts and caveats, and both said what they changed. A stayed closer to the original wording, though it did add a title and turned 'Not covered' into a heading. B also changed meaning-bearing words ('probably' to 'may', 'see' to 'note'), and it justified the first change by citing 'two of six', which misreads the 4 of 6 / 2 of 4 finding. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers keep every count and caveat, add a title and bold headings, and list their changes. A also swaps 'probably' for 'may' and 'see' for 'note', which changes the author's judgment and goes beyond a light polish; its reason ('two of six is thin evidence') also misreads the data. B leaves the findings and caveats exactly as written and only changes formatting and punctuation, though it does add a title and turns 'Not covered' into a heading.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers add a title, rewrite the intro line and bold the headers, so neither is a truly minimal edit. B makes more changes to content. It drops 'said', which turns a self-report into a fact. It also swaps 'probably' for 'may', which changes the user's own hedge, yet B claims the content is unchanged. A keeps every claim and caveat as written and lists its edits fairly accurately, though it doesn't mention the title it added. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B stays closer to the original. It keeps 'probably' and 'said they didn't know', so the reported claim stays attributed to participants. A drops 'said', which turns what two participants reported into a flat fact, and it swaps the user's hedge for its own. However, B doesn't mention that it added a title and rewrote the intro, and its note about making '1 of 6' consistent describes no real change, so A's account of its changes is more accurate.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers add a title and rework the intro, but B keeps the substance exactly as written. That includes 'said they didn't know' and the user's own 'probably'. A silently drops 'said', which turns a self-report into a stated fact. It also changes 'probably' to 'may' and 'see' to 'note', and its change list doesn't mention dropping 'said'. B's one overreach is turning 'Not covered' into its own section, which is minor. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A keeps the wording and caveats and only changes formatting and contractions, and its list of changes is accurate, though making 'Not covered' its own section adds a small heading. Answer B drops 'said', so what two users reported becomes a stated fact. It also changes 'probably' to 'may' without being asked. Its change list misstates which sentence was split, doesn't mention removing 'said', and wrongly claims the content was left as written.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give the same correct statistics (z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, CI about −0.7 to +1.7 points, about 23k visitors per arm), and both refuse to call B the winner. B gives more practical help with the boss: a ready-made status line, three clear Friday options and a guardrail check before shipping. Its traffic figure is slightly off, though: about 950 per day per arm assumes two days, when it said two and a half. Neither answer explicitly says to check the traffic split or the tracking, and A is a little more compact. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use the same correct statistics (z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.42, a confidence interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23k visitors per variant), and neither suggests checking that the traffic split and tracking worked. B is somewhat better on handling the boss: it says to set the end date now and not stop early, and it warns against presenting the 14% relative lift to the board, explaining the credibility cost if the result doesn't hold. A's guardrail-metric check is useful, but it is not a check of the split or tracking.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers get the core statistics right: z ≈ 0.8, p ≈ 0.4, a 95% CI of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23–24k visitors per variant needed. Both also warn against peeking and against calling B a winner. B estimates traffic more accurately (about 760 per variant per day over roughly 2.5 days, versus A's 950). B also at least flags the 50/50 split assumption, though neither explicitly recommends checking the split or the tracking. B handles the boss better: it suggests keeping a holdout if shipping, and it points out that the risk lies in the claim to the board, not in the button itself. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the statistics right: p ≈ 0.42, a 95% interval of about −0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 23–24k visitors needed per variant. Both refuse to call B the winner and give honest wording for the board. A is more compact and adds a practical holdout option. It also makes the point that the risk lies in the claim to the board, not the button change, and it at least flags the 50/50 split assumption. Neither answer clearly says to check the split ratio and the purchase tracking.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers give correct numbers: p ≈ 0.42, a confidence interval of about -0.7 to +1.7 points, and roughly 20–24k visitors needed per arm. Both also give the boss a workable plan: ship as a judgment call, but don't tell the board B 'won'. B is better because it checks that the 50/50 split held, that visitors stay in one variant, that the metric was chosen before the test, and that the stop date is written down. A says to set the run length in advance but never checks that the split or tracking worked. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers get the statistics right (p ≈ 0.42, 95% CI about -0.7 to +1.7 points, roughly 23–24k visitors per arm needed), and both give sensible ways to handle the boss and the board. A wins because it also says to check that the split is about 50/50, that visitors stay in one variant, and that the metric was chosen before the test started. B never mentions checking the split or the tracking. B's traffic estimate (about 750 per variant per day) is closer to the real pace than A's (850–950), and its options are a little richer, but A is tighter and covers the full rubric.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers turn down the fake interviews, give labeled hypothesis personas with illustrative quotes, and suggest quick real conversations before Thursday. Both footers claim the personas are 'based on market research/data' even though no research was done. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B states plainly that it won't write the personas as interview findings, while A only says it would 'steer you away' from that framing. Both give a short, sound reason, provide pasteable hypothesis slides with quotes marked illustrative, and suggest real calls before Thursday. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give a concrete ranked layout, put the seat picker and the screen-reader block at the top, and present counts as n of 5. A also says more about the limits of the sample, such as how participants were recruited and not generalizing beyond first-time visitors. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers rank the seat picker and the screen-reader block at the top and keep colors and the date picker low. B gives a more concrete layout, with explicit columns for count, observation, severity and evidence strength. It also says outright to keep proposed fixes out of the findings, and it justifies the screen-reader item as a total failure on a core task. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B wins narrowly. Its consent step is stronger: it asks for spoken permission to record, says who will hear it, and says to wait for a clear yes before recording. B also stays tightly on the last real rental, and its 'Swap these out' box shows how to turn leading questions into neutral ones. A covers 'not selling' (B misses this) but never says 'not testing', and a few of its questions lean toward negatives ('was a hassle', 'trust... enough to pay'). Both screenshots are cut off at the bottom, so neither can be confirmed to fit on one printed page. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A has a clearer spoken consent: it says 'I'm not testing you', asks permission to record and tells the interviewer to wait for a yes before recording, but it never says the interviewer isn't selling anything. Answer B says 'I'm not selling' but folds recording into a quick parenthetical and doesn't say the participant isn't being tested; its two-column layout is denser and harder to scan while talking. Both stay focused on the last real rental, have times that add up to 40 minutes and don't invent any data, but both screenshots look like they may run past one page.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B keeps every question on real past events, including the last rental, a time something went wrong and the last time they compared places. It also has a fuller consent checklist and a 'Don't' list that targets hypotheticals and leading wording. A is well organized and its times add up, but its 'Tools & expectations' section asks a hypothetical about what renters would expect online. Each opening misses one required point: A never says the participant isn't being tested, and B never says the interviewer isn't selling anything. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A keeps every question tied to real past experience and has no leading or hypothetical prompts. Its spoken intro covers consent, recording and 'I'm not testing you', but it never tells the participant 'I'm not selling anything' (it only reminds the interviewer not to pitch). B's intro says 'not selling anything' and asks to record, but section 4 opens with the leading 'most annoying or confusing part', and section 5 asks hypothetical expectation questions and invites showing Paddlepoint. Both time plans add up to 40 minutes. B's two-column layout is denser and looks likely to run past one printed page.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B has a fuller spoken consent and recording statement, including who will hear the recording and how it is stored, plus a pre-recording checklist. Its questions stay more consistently on the last real experience, while A's 'Wishes' section brings in hypothetical questions. Neither answer fully covers item 1: A says 'not selling anything' but not 'not being tested', and B says the reverse. A prints a bit cleaner and has more whitespace, but B is stronger on research method and probes. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A has a fuller spoken consent and recording script (it says who will listen, how long it's kept and how data is anonymized, and asks for a clear yes). Its questions stay on the last real rental and avoid leading wording. B says the user isn't selling anything, but its recording consent is a passing aside, and its 'Wishes' section asks hypothetical questions. B's 'Was there a time booking was a hassle' also leans leading. Both splits add up to 40 minutes and both include neutral probes. B's layout is a little more spacious, while A's footer is dense.
